content:
Hi, all. I am trying to build an incremental computation library in Lean based off of the Jane Street incremental library.

I am very new to functional programming and proof assistants. My motivation for this project is downstream of a need to build a high-performance domain-specific incremental (technically, self-adjusting) computation system for a JIT compiled language. Since I anticipate that project getting very complicated, I am interested in using Lean as an FP lang to specify the algorithms of that upcoming app-specific incremental system and then using the theorem-proving side of Lean to prove the correctness of the hideous optimizations we doubtlessly will have to implement. The production implementation will likely be done in Rust or C.

As I said, I don't have much experience with FP (other than having done most of Functional Programming in Lean) and have zero experience with theorem proving, so I don't know if the expectations stated above for using Lean are realistic, particularly the verification goals. Hence the desire to do a simpler project first as a trial run.

My questions for the Lean community as I introduce myself are:

  1. What do you think is the right place to get started with DAGs in Lean for my use case? I am not interested in proving new ideas in graph theory, so is mathlib's SimpleGraph not useful to me? Should I create my own DAG structure? For context, incremental computation systems (including Jane Street's which I want to clone for this trial run) are generally centered around dependency graphs of computation. My experience working in graphs has been in Rust's petgraph, Python's NetworkX, and JS's Cytoscape.
  2. Do you think my objectives for using Lean as a theorem prover to prove the correctness of an incremental computation system is realistic? The crux of the proof is going to be that the "work-skipping" pipelines produce the same outcome as if none of the work-skipping pipelines were used.

I'll note I have not been very successful at navigating the mathlib API docs or Loogle, LeanExplore, and LeanDojo, so if anyone has recommendations for being more self-sufficient with the existing Lean docs/tools for someone whose background is neither mathematics nor theory-heavy CS, please tell me! I'm very grateful for your feedback!

One note is that docs#SimpleGraph and docs#Digraph are encoded as a relation, so if you need to to high performance graph operations (rather than just proving theorems about them) these types might not be suitable. E.g. I think if you take the union of two graphs it has to redo that computation every time you want to check whether an edge exists. There's also docs#Graph, but that doesn't seem to be set up with computability in mind.

That being said, if you are verifying code that works with graphs in another language, that doesn't necessarily mean you need to do fast computations on graphs within Lean.
Try inductive tree types with node IDs.
I used that trick to encode circuits.
Treat nodes with identical IDs as identical nodes.
